frictionVectors.title: European gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian pipeline gas while pressing Algiers on migration, regional security, and market access. Algeria is using export diversification and long-term contracts to preserve bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara alignment
frictionVectors.details: Algeria's support for Sahrawi self-determination continues to drive strategic friction with Morocco and complicate Maghreb infrastructure and energy integration.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain central to Angola's transport and energy infrastructure, constraining fiscal flexibility despite debt-restructuring efforts and diversification plans.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining production, foreign-operated offshore assets, and exposure to global price cycles limit Luanda's effective control over its main strategic revenue stream.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Cotonou and northbound trade corridors are attracting regional and external investment, but dependence on foreign capital and neighboring market access creates strategic vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the northern borders threatens transport routes, agricultural zones, and state control over emerging resource corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial leverage over diamond extraction and marketing, but demand volatility and dependence on major international trading networks expose public revenues to external shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals is growing, creating opportunities for diversification while testing Botswana's regulatory capacity and local-beneficiation ambitions.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control
frictionVectors.details: The state is seeking greater control over gold production and licensing, but informal mining, smuggling networks, and insecurity continue to divert value from public revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from French military cooperation toward Russian-linked security support increases Ouagadougou's room for maneuver but introduces opacity, reputational costs, and new dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: Bujumbura is seeking greater state control and revenue from nickel, gold, and rare-earth prospects, but limited infrastructure and opaque licensing leave room for foreign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over accusations of supporting armed groups, while Burundi balances regional security commitments with dependence on external aid and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Connectivity Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde retains strong regulatory control, but its ports, digital infrastructure, and energy systems depend heavily on European, American, and Chinese financing.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to external tourism cycles and imported fuel costs, limiting practical sovereignty despite stable institutions and diversified partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms remain central to oil, gas, timber, and emerging mining projects, while infrastructure and revenue arrangements often provide limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Sahel Instability
frictionVectors.details: The Anglophone conflict and attacks linked to Boko Haram and other armed groups weaken state control over transport corridors and border economies, increasing reliance on external security support.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-for-Resources Model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel remain influential around the regime, while gold and diamond networks operate amid weak oversight and limited transparency over commercial concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country depends on fragile routes through Cameroon and neighboring states for fuel, trade, and humanitarian access, leaving infrastructure and sovereignty exposed to regional actors.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil Revenue Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal sovereignty remains tied to oil production and export infrastructure controlled through foreign commercial and financing relationships, constraining policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Sudan and Libya, together with persistent internal insurgent threats, drives reliance on foreign military and intelligence partnerships during a sensitive political transition.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime jurisdiction
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with France over Mayotte continues to constrain Comoros's territorial sovereignty and complicate migration and maritime-security policy.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on external finance
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic revenues leave infrastructure and energy projects dependent on France, Gulf partners, and multilateral donors, reducing policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain major influence in copper and cobalt processing, while Western and Gulf actors seek alternative access, leaving Kinshasa balancing contracts, sovereignty, and investment needs.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern security and regional interference
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving armed groups and suspected external backing disrupts mining zones, border trade, and transport infrastructure, weakening central control over resources.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the core source of foreign exchange and fiscal power, exposing the country to production shocks and limiting diversification of sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-access bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for roads, ports, and energy, but repayment obligations and project terms can narrow Brazzaville's negotiating autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa-sector value leakage
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire has strengthened producer oversight and processing ambitions, but international buyers and volatile prices still capture substantial value beyond the state and farming sector.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital and strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Major port, energy, and transport projects rely on multinational and external financing, creating growth while generating long-term exposure to foreign commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military-base competition
frictionVectors.details: US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military presences generate revenue and deterrence but make Djibouti's sovereignty highly dependent on rival external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Control of ports and logistics infrastructure is central to the economy, while debt and commercial dependence on external lenders—especially China—limit fiscal flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and asset dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs have increased reliance on Gulf investment, multilateral lenders, and strategic asset sales. This can dilute Cairo's policy autonomy in ports, infrastructure, and energy.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and Red Sea insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, while attacks and instability around the Red Sea threaten Suez Canal revenues and maritime security.

highlights: Malabo seeks new gas and mineral partners

frictionVectors.title: Maturing energy assets
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil production and limited diversification leave the state vulnerable to foreign operators, volatile prices, and declining fiscal income. New gas projects may extend revenue but do not yet resolve structural dependence.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for major infrastructure, creating repayment and strategic-dependence risks as hydrocarbon revenues weaken.

highlights: Mining remains the principal foreign-exchange engine

frictionVectors.title: Mining concentration
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide critical revenue but leave Eritrea dependent on a narrow set of foreign mining relationships and commodity markets.

frictionVectors.title: Regional militarization
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Ethiopia, Sudan, and Red Sea security continue to expose Eritrea to external pressure and constrain autonomous economic development.

highlights: Sugar and manufacturing remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Economic dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport, electricity, and investment links with South Africa provide stability but sharply limit Eswatini's room for independent economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Fiscal and infrastructure vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Southern African Customs Union receipts and external infrastructure finance leaves the kingdom exposed to regional downturns and shifting donor or investor priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam enhances domestic power and export potential but remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operations, and water security.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign financing and market access
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and dependence on international lenders, China, Gulf investors, and development partners constrain Addis Ababa's ability to direct infrastructure and industrial policy independently.

highlights: Oil, manganese and timber remain strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: Resource renegotiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater domestic value capture from manganese, oil and timber while managing dependence on foreign operators and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: External influence rebalancing
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is diversifying longstanding French ties toward American, Chinese and regional partners, creating uncertainty over infrastructure financing and strategic access.

highlights: Ports and roads attract competing partners

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Banjul and transport links remain central to trade but require foreign capital, leaving the country exposed to financing conditions and neighboring Senegal's economic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew and fishing sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign buyers and fishing fleets capture substantial value from agriculture and marine resources, while enforcement capacity limits the state's ability to secure local benefits.

highlights: Gold and bauxite remain sovereignty tests

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Accra is seeking more domestic processing and stronger terms in gold, bauxite and manganese, but fiscal pressure increases reliance on multinational investors and external lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and Chinese, Gulf and Western financing are stabilizing the economy while narrowing room for autonomous spending on ports, energy and transport.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project is drawing major Chinese and international capital, but rail, port and local-content arrangements will determine whether Guinea captures durable sovereign value.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque contract governance
frictionVectors.details: Military rule has increased state control over mining administration while limiting transparency, raising risks of elite capture, labor unrest and externally driven concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Cocaine-transit vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak enforcement and porous maritime routes continue to expose the country to transnational trafficking networks, external criminal influence and corruption within state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-funded infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, roads and energy projects depend heavily on outside donors and investors, while political instability reduces the government's bargaining power over contracts and natural resources.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and Port Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is seeking greater fiscal and operational flexibility over Chinese-financed transport assets while preserving access to external capital. Mombasa and the Standard Gauge Railway remain sensitive symbols of infrastructure sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu Port–South Sudan–Ethiopia corridor offers strategic leverage but faces insecurity, regional rivalry, and uncertain commercial demand. Gulf, Chinese, and Western partners are competing for influence around logistics and energy links.

frictionVectors.title: South African Control of Water Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho’s fiscal position and infrastructure development remain closely tied to water sales to South Africa through the Lesotho Highlands Water Project. Delays, cost overruns, and unequal bargaining power constrain national control over this strategic resource.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Owned Industrial Base
frictionVectors.details: The textile sector and major construction projects depend heavily on foreign investors and preferential trade access. This creates employment but leaves Lesotho exposed to external decisions on sourcing, tariffs, and capital allocation.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Liberia’s fiscal and export prospects remain strongly tied to large foreign-operated iron ore concessions, particularly around rail and port access. The government faces pressure to improve local value capture without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Rail-Port Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Control of mineral transport corridors and Buchanan-linked export infrastructure gives concessionaires substantial bargaining power. Competition among Western, Chinese, and regional investors could expand Liberia’s options but also deepen dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest control over production, exports, and public revenue flows. Periodic blockades and institutional disputes leave Libya’s primary resource vulnerable to domestic factional and external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Turkish and Russian Strategic Footprints
frictionVectors.details: Turkey retains major influence in western Libya through security and maritime arrangements, while Russia-linked forces maintain leverage in the east and south. Their presence affects energy routes, military infrastructure, and Libya’s ability to pursue an autonomous foreign policy.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining, including the Ambatovy operation, provides export revenue but leaves Madagascar exposed to foreign ownership, commodity cycles, and limited domestic processing. Negotiations over fiscal terms and environmental obligations remain central to resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Corridor Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, roads, and power systems serving mining projects compete with broader national development needs. Foreign-financed infrastructure can improve capacity while reinforcing enclave-style extraction and local environmental tensions.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking investment in uranium, rare earths and graphite, but financing and technical dependence give external firms substantial leverage over project terms and export value.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND TRANSPORT BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and weak rail connectivity limit domestic processing and increase reliance on foreign-funded infrastructure and regional corridors.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SOVEREIGNTY AND SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are seeking greater state control and local processing of gold, while insecurity, informal production and foreign commercial interests continue to complicate revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: SANCTIONS AND REGIONAL CORRIDORS
frictionVectors.details: Breakdown with regional institutions and strained relations with Western partners raise the cost of trade, energy supply and access to coastal export routes.

highlights: Iron and gas strengthen bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: GAS REVENUE AND DEVELOPMENT TERMS
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project offers new revenue and regional leverage, but offshore operations and marketing remain heavily dependent on international partners.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE LOGISTICS
frictionVectors.details: The state is pursuing downstream processing and rail expansion, yet the mining economy remains concentrated around foreign-linked operators and a single vulnerable export corridor.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS AND MARITIME SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to press its claim over the Chagos Archipelago while navigating security, access and diplomatic interests involving the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DIGITAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Expansion as an Indian Ocean logistics and data hub brings investment and influence from India, China and Gulf states, requiring careful balancing of strategic infrastructure ownership.

highlights: Industrial policy deepens domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE AND GREEN INDUSTRY CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Morocco retains strong state influence over phosphates while attracting foreign partners into fertilizer, renewables and green hydrogen, creating tension between capital access and domestic value retention.

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy and mineral projects linked to Western Sahara strengthen Rabat's logistical position but remain exposed to diplomatic disputes, legal challenges and regional opposition.

highlights: LNG ambitions constrained by Cabo Delgado insecurity
Resource nationalism rises around foreign gas projects

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten LNG infrastructure and delays the restoration of full-scale offshore projects. Maputo remains reliant on foreign security assistance and energy partners.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International gas companies and lenders retain substantial leverage over project terms, while public expectations for jobs and revenue-sharing are rising.

highlights: Green hydrogen strategy faces execution pressure

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Namibia is seeking greater domestic value addition and bargaining power as foreign firms develop uranium, lithium, and other strategic deposits. Infrastructure and financing needs still limit state leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed hydrogen proposals could diversify the economy but may reproduce enclave-style extraction unless local procurement, water security, and fiscal returns are firmly protected.

highlights: Junta tightens control over extractive sectors
Western security ties replaced by diversified partnerships

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pressing foreign operators for greater state participation and revenue, increasing uncertainty around existing mining agreements and export continuity.

frictionVectors.title: Security and Transit Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence, regional diplomatic tensions, and reduced Western cooperation threaten mining corridors and raise dependence on alternative external security and infrastructure partners.

highlights: Gas and power infrastructure bottlenecks persist

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria retains major formal control over hydrocarbons, but foreign capital, technical dependence, theft, and opaque contracting continue to dilute effective sovereign capture of value.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Pipeline Security
frictionVectors.details: Grid weakness, pipeline vandalism, and insecurity constrain industrial growth and export reliability, leaving the state dependent on external finance and operators for infrastructure upgrades.

highlights: Regional security posture raises external pressure

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Accusations of support for the M23 rebellion continue to generate diplomatic and economic pressure, complicating Rwanda's regional trade and security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda maintains strong control over domestic development priorities, but donor scrutiny and dependence on foreign investment create exposure when governance or regional-security disputes intensify.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Licensing Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Unproven hydrocarbon prospects attract outside interest, but limited exploration capacity and weak fiscal leverage constrain São Tomé and Príncipe's ability to set terms.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on external finance, imported fuel, and foreign-linked maritime infrastructure leaves the country vulnerable to donor and investor priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Contract Renegotiation Risk
frictionVectors.details: The government's sovereignty agenda is seeking greater national returns from oil, gas, and mining projects, creating friction with international operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing Access Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing by foreign fleets remains politically sensitive as Senegal balances food security, coastal livelihoods, and revenue from access agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tuna access fees and foreign fleets provide essential revenue but limit national control over marine resources and increase pressure on fisheries management.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on partners for maritime surveillance and infrastructure, requiring careful balancing among India, European states, China, and other security actors.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Rutile Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked mining operations dominate export earnings, while the state continues to face challenges securing stronger local processing, taxation, and employment benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and Port Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors and port infrastructure give external operators significant influence over logistics and export conditions, limiting broader national value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Hydrocarbon Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Offshore exploration and licensing involve foreign capital and technical operators while federal-state disputes and weak oversight complicate Somalia's control of prospective resources.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Port and Security Patrons
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, neighboring countries, and other external actors compete for port, security, and maritime influence, often outpacing Somalia's institutional capacity to coordinate terms.

frictionVectors.title: GRID AND LOGISTICS CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and rail-port congestion continue to reduce South Africa's ability to capture value from minerals domestically. Private investment is expanding, but infrastructure control remains fragmented and politically contested.

frictionVectors.title: COMPETING EXTERNAL MINERALS PARTNERSHIPS
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, the European Union and Gulf investors are competing for influence over battery minerals, energy and logistics. Pretoria is seeking strategic autonomy through diversified partnerships and BRICS ties.

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE AND EXPORT VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports rely on infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving revenues exposed to pipeline damage, transit disputes and external security risks. The government has limited alternatives for monetizing crude.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN OIL AND SECURITY LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: International oil firms and regional actors retain substantial influence over production, transport and payments. Weak institutions and elite competition limit public control over resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND ARMED-ACTOR ECONOMIES
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling provide vital financing to competing military networks and intermediaries. External buyers and regional commercial channels can extract value while bypassing accountable state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND INFRASTRUCTURE CONTEST
frictionVectors.details: Control of Red Sea ports, transport corridors and energy infrastructure is strategically tied to the war. Gulf, Russian and other foreign interests are positioned to shape postwar access, reconstruction and maritime security.

highlights: LNG and rail corridors advance unevenly

frictionVectors.title: LNG DEVELOPMENT AND CONTRACT CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Long-delayed offshore gas development offers major revenue potential but raises disputes over fiscal terms, local content and environmental safeguards. Foreign energy companies retain significant technical and financial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Investment in Dar es Salaam and regional rail corridors is increasing Tanzania's strategic importance while intensifying scrutiny of foreign operators and concession terms. The government is balancing capital access against fears of losing control over critical gateways.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN OPERATORS
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is central to Togo's trade and regional influence, but its expansion depends on foreign capital, logistics expertise and shipping networks. This creates exposure to external commercial pressure over tariffs, concessions and access.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability from the Sahel are pushing Togo to strengthen border security and external defense partnerships. Security dependence could constrain Lomé's room for maneuver among regional and international actors.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation remain closely linked, limiting Tunisian policy autonomy while domestic fiscal pressures constrain bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Energy sovereignty gap
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on imported hydrocarbons and external power arrangements, while declining investment and strained public finances slow renewable and grid development.

highlights: Oil future tied to foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and environmental dispute
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains strategically important but faces Western banking, legal, and environmental pressure, increasing reliance on Chinese and other non-Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-led infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Road, energy, and oil infrastructure is being developed through external finance and contractors, creating long-term repayment and revenue-sharing exposure before production begins.

frictionVectors.title: Copper value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is attracting competing Western, Gulf, and Chinese interest in copper and critical minerals, but limited domestic refining and processing leave much of the value captured abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Mining fiscal and power pressures
frictionVectors.details: Tax disputes, electricity shortages, and infrastructure bottlenecks complicate efforts to convert rising mineral demand into durable sovereign revenue and local industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors remain prominent in lithium, platinum, and gold, while Zimbabwe seeks greater local processing without sufficient domestic capital or technology.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions, restricted access to finance, and persistent currency instability increase dependence on bilateral investors and commodity-backed arrangements, weakening negotiating leverage.
